literary_identity: English essayist, poet, dramatist, and Whig politician who, with Richard Steele, created the periodical essay and shaped Augustan letters.
biography: Born at Milston in Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman, Addison was educated at the Charterhouse and at Queen's College, Oxford, where he became a fellow. Early Latin and English verse won him patronage, and he travelled on the Continent before returning to public life. With Richard Steele he wrote for the Tatler and then founded the Spectator, which established the modern periodical essay. His blank-verse tragedy Cato (1713) was widely performed and admired. He held government posts, including a secretaryship of state, as a prominent Whig, and edited the Whig journal the Guardian. He died in London in 1719.
literary_profile: Best remembered as a moral essayist and critic of taste whose Spectator papers observe manners, commerce, reading, and sociability with urbanity and restraint. He also wrote neoclassical tragedy and didactic and occasional verse.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, balanced, conversational prose in the middle style; a temperate, courteous humour; aphoristic moral reflection; and a preference for good sense, decorum, and polished plainness over extravagance.
intellectual_concerns: Cultivation of polite sociability and taste; the moral duties of commercial and leisure classes; religion regulated by reason; classical learning made accessible; and the refinement of public manners through letters.
historical_significance: Co-creator of the periodical essay, a form that influenced eighteenth-century prose, journalism, and the idea of a reading public; Cato was a model of neoclassical English tragedy and a lasting political emblem.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth date is recorded, though the precise circumstances of his Oxford fellowship and his share of authorship in the joint periodicals with Steele remain debated by scholars.

literary_identity: Anglo-Irish-born essayist, dramatist, and Whig publicist who founded the Tatler and co-founded the Spectator with Joseph Addison.
biography: Born in Dublin and raised partly in England, Steele was educated at the Charterhouse and entered the army, buying a commission. He turned to writing and in 1709 founded the Tatler, a daily periodical of essays and news, soon joined by Addison. In 1711 the two launched the Spectator, to which Steele also contributed essays of feeling and reform. He wrote sentimental comedy, most successfully The Conscious Lovers (1722), and several political journals. A Whig member of Parliament, he fell into debt and estrangement from Addison in later life. After illness he retired to Wales, where he died in 1729.
literary_profile: A writer of familiar prose and sentimental drama, more impulsive and emotionally warm than Addison, who used the periodical to promote benevolence, fashion reform, and domestic feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Open, affectionate, sometimes hurried prose; a strong appeal to the heart rather than to judgement; lively character sketches; and an earnest, confessing moral voice.
intellectual_concerns: Reform of manners and duelling; benevolence and filial duty; Whig politics and religious toleration; and the sentimental education of the middle-class reader.
historical_significance: Inventor of the periodical essay through the Tatler and joint founder of the Spectator; a pioneer of sentimental comedy whose The Conscious Lovers dominated early eighteenth-century stage reform.
biographical_uncertainty: His year and circumstances of birth are uncertain and commonly given only as about 1672; the precise division of labour between him and Addison in the Tatler and Spectator is still disputed.

literary_identity: English poet, satirist, and translator, the dominant verse mind of Augustan England and a leading figure of the heroic-couplet tradition.
biography: Born in London into a Roman Catholic family, Pope was largely self-educated because his faith barred him from the universities, and lifelong ill health confined him much to the countryside at Windsor and later Twickenham. An early Essay on Criticism (1711) established his reputation, followed by the mock-heroic Rape of the Lock (1712, expanded 1714). Between 1715 and 1720 he published a celebrated verse translation of the Iliad, financed by subscription. His political and personal satires culminated in the Dunciad (1728, revised 1743), and his philosophical poem An Essay on Man appeared in 1733-1734. He died at Twickenham in 1744.
literary_profile: A poet of satire, epistle, and translation who perfected the closed heroic couplet and made verse the instrument of social and intellectual criticism; his work ranges from elegant ridicule to sustained moral philosophy.
stylistic_characteristics: Epigrammatic compression and antithesis in the heroic couplet; balanced syntax, precise rhyme, and pointed wit; a commanding satiric voice; and a neoclassical polish that subordinates invention to judgement.
intellectual_concerns: Order amid social and literary chaos; the limits and uses of reason; self-knowledge and self-interest in society; the corruption of taste and learning; and the poet's relation to patronage and the market.
historical_significance: The central English poet of the early eighteenth century and the standard-bearer of the neoclassical heroic couplet; his satires and criticism defined Augustan literary culture and influenced prose style for decades.
biographical_uncertainty: A frail, deformed body and his Roman Catholicism shaped his life; some details of his schooling and the dating of his early poems are reconstructed from family and manuscript evidence rather than firm records.

literary_identity: Anglo-Irish satirist, pamphleteer, and cleric, Dean of St Patrick's Dublin, widely regarded as the greatest prose satirist in English.
biography: Born in Dublin, Swift was educated at Trinity College Dublin and took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He worked in London as secretary to Sir William Temple and later sought Anglican preferment, aligning with the Tories as editor of the Examiner. His political and literary writings include the Battle of the Books (1704), the Bickerstaff pamphlets, and A Tale of a Tub (1704). The Drapier's Letters (1724) made him a popular hero in Ireland for resisting Wood's halfpence. His masterpiece, Gulliver's Travels, appeared in 1726, followed by the Modest Proposal (1729). In his last years a probable illness impaired his speech and memory; he died in Dublin in 1745.
literary_profile: A prose satirist and moralist whose range runs from savage irony to learned parody and invective; he wrote fiction, pamphlets, sermons, journals, and verse, always in service of unmasking pride, folly, and abuse of power.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, concrete style he prized, with short clauses and deadpan seriousness; sustained irony and personation; grotesque and anatomical imagery; and a harsh, uncompromising satiric logic.
intellectual_concerns: The pride and rationalisation of humankind; the abuse of learning, religion, and language; English domination of Ireland and political corruption; and the tension between reason and the passions.
historical_significance: The foremost English-language satirist and a defining prose stylist; Gulliver's Travels and the Modest Proposal became touchstones of satire, and his Irish writings shaped modern Irish political consciousness.
biographical_uncertainty: The diagnosis of his later mental and physical decline is uncertain and retrospectively labelled by modern physicians; his parentage and early years in Dublin are partly known only from contested accounts.

literary_identity: English poet and dramatist, friend of Pope and Swift, best known for the ballad opera The Beggar's Opera and his Fables.
biography: Born in Devon and apprenticed to a silkseller in London, Gay attached himself to the Augustan literary circle, befriending Pope, Swift, and John Arbuthnot, and joining the Scriblerus Club. Early poems such as Rural Sports, also called Trivia (1716), won notice. He wrote for the theatre in various modes, including pastoral and burlesque tragedy. His The Beggar's Opera (1728), a ballad opera satirising politics and the stage, was a great success and provoked political controversy that helped block his sequel Polly. His Fables, first and second collections appearing in 1727 and posthumously in 1738, remain famous. He died in London in 1732.
literary_profile: A versatile versifier and dramatist working in georgic, pastoral, fable, and burlesque, whose enduring achievements are the satiric ballad opera and the morally pointed fable.
stylistic_characteristics: Lucid, unambitious Augustan diction; ease in popular and borrowed airs; epigrammatic moralising in the fables; and a genial, often sly satire rather than Swiftian ferocity.
intellectual_concerns: The corruption beneath social polish; the economics of crime and respectability; the rivalry between Italian opera and native drama; and the conduct of ordinary life as illustrated by beast-fable.
historical_significance: Inventor of the ballad opera with The Beggar's Opera, a landmark that reshaped English musical theatre and literary satire of manners, and a leading fabulist of his generation.
biographical_uncertainty: His exact year of birth is not recorded and is given as about 1685; the chronology of his early poems and plays rests partly on manuscript and dedicatory evidence.

literary_identity: Anglo-Irish poet and Anglican clergyman, a friend of Pope and a member of the Scriblerus Club, admired for his meditative and light verse.
biography: Parnell was an Irish scholar, commonly held to have been born about 1679 and educated at Trinity College Dublin, where he took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He rose to hold benefices near Dublin and was archdeacon of Glendalough. Close to Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift, he joined the Scriblerus Club, and Pope borrowed the theme of his own early Pastoral from Parnell's The Hermit. His short poems circulated in manuscript and periodicals during his lifetime, and a collected Poetical Works appeared posthumously in 1721. He died in Dublin in 1718.
literary_profile: A poet of modest output but high reputation, best known for a single reflective piece, The Hermit, together with light, witty songs and hymns that display ease and quiet moral feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Smooth Augustan couplets and lyric measures; a calm, meditative tone; graceful wit; and a plainness and sweetness praised by Pope as a model of true ease.
intellectual_concerns: Quietist contentment and retirement; moral self-examination; religious resignation; and the pleasantries and vanities of social life.
historical_significance: A transitional poet whose The Hermit anticipated the grave-mediation and churchyard current of later eighteenth-century verse, and a valued link within the Pope and Swift circle.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is uncertain and given as about 1679; some details of his Irish benefices and his family background rest on later biographical tradition.

literary_identity: English dramatist, poet, and editor, appointed Poet Laureate in 1715, celebrated for sentimental tragedy and an early scholarly edition of Shakespeare.
biography: Rowe was educated at the Middle Temple and turned early to the stage. His first play, The Ambitious Statesman (1697), was followed by Jane Shore (1700) and The Fair Penitent (1703), the latter containing the villain Lothaire and often considered his finest. He wrote several further tragedies, including a Lucius Junius Brutus and a Lady Jane Grey. In 1709 he published an edition of Shakespeare, an early largely scholarly attempt to edit the plays and to give accounts of the actors, drawing on earlier sources and issued through the publisher Jacob Tonson. A Whig, he succeeded Thomas Tate as Poet Laureate in 1715 and died unexpectedly in London at the end of 1718.
literary_profile: A playwright of domestic and sentimental tragedy and a literary editor; his dramas turn on female virtue, seduction, and penitence, and his Shakespeare edition began the formal text-critical study of the plays.
stylistic_characteristics: Smooth, decorous blank verse; moralising pathos; well-made tragic situations; and an editorial method marked by conjectural emendation and a taste for regularity and probability.
intellectual_concerns: Virtue under assault and the ethics of penitence; domestic and feminine suffering; national literary heritage and the canonisation of Shakespeare; and Whig political virtue.
historical_significance: His 1709 Shakespeare is a founding document of English literary scholarship and editing, and as laureate and dramatist he shaped early eighteenth-century taste in tragedy and commemorative verse.
major_influences: Jacob Tonson and the publishing trade
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace is not securely recorded; Rowe is associated with places in Buckinghamshire and the south, and the precise location of his birth remains uncertain.

literary_identity: Scottish-born poet, best known for the blank-verse landscape cycle The Seasons, who helped introduce descriptive and sensuous nature poetry to English verse.
biography: Thomson was born in the Scottish borders, the son of a minister, and studied divinity at the University of Edinburgh before abandoning the church for letters in London. He supported himself by tutoring and writing, and published Winter in 1726, soon expanding his descriptive pieces into The Seasons in its four-part edition of 1730. He wrote political and patriotic dramas, including Sophonisba (1730), and the Liberty poems (1734-1736). He enjoyed patronage associated with the Prince of Wales's circle at Leicester. He died suddenly in London in 1748.
literary_profile: A poet of nature, sensation, and civic patriotism; his central work observes the changing seasons in rich descriptive blank verse and infuses landscape with emotional and moral reflection.
stylistic_characteristics: Sensuous, pictorial blank verse in long descriptive passages; accumulation of visual and atmospheric detail; a meditative, sometimes rapturous tone; and Miltonic diction and inversion.
intellectual_concerns: Nature as spectacle and moral teacher; the senses and the passions; British liberty, trade, and empire; the pleasure of the sublime and the picturesque; and the relation of landscape to feeling.
historical_significance: The Seasons transformed English nature poetry and anticipated the Romantic sensibility and the picturesque; it was one of the most influential and often-set poetic works of the eighteenth century.

literary_identity: English physician and ambitious religious epic poet, remembered chiefly as a target of Pope's satire in the Dunciad.
biography: Blackmore was born in the west of England about 1654 and studied medicine at Exeter College, Oxford, taking his medical degree there and becoming a fellow of the College of Physicians. He practised as a physician in the west country and then in London, and was physician to William III. He published a long sacred epic, Creation (1712), a paraphrase of Job, and a sequel Paradise Regain'd (1718), together with poems on the mind and nature and medical and philosophical writings. His grand but heavily moralising verse drew ridicule from his rivals, and Pope mocked him in the Dunciad. He died in 1729.
literary_profile: A writer of didactic and religious epic who sought to render Miltonic verse into sober Protestant instruction; his ambition was greater than his reception.
stylistic_characteristics: Weighty, moralising blank verse; elaborate scientific and theological paraphrase; a plain earnestness and diffuseness that contemporaries found tedious; and an addiction to poetic machinery of the mind.
intellectual_concerns: Providence, creation, and sacred history; the relation of medicine, body, and soul; natural philosophy and vitalism; and the defence of a pious, learned verse against the wit of the age.
historical_significance: A representative of the earnest sacred-epic and physico-theological tradition that his Augustan rivals displaced; his treatment in the Dunciad helped fix his posterity as a cautionary figure of misapplied ambition.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is given only as about 1654, and his exact birthplace in the west of England is not firmly established; the chronology of his medical career and publications is partly reconstructed.

literary_identity: English poet and essayist, Regius Professor of Civil Law at Oxford, whose meditative Night Thoughts and critical Conjectures made him a precursor of Romantic sensibility.
biography: Young was born in Hampshire, educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and became a fellow, later holding the Regius Professorship of Civil Law. His early verse included a poem on Parliament, and he wrote occasional and festival verse before settling into his characteristic meditative mode. After years of relative quiet he published The Complainture, or Night Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality (1742-1745), which made his name through its meditations on grief after family bereavements. Later nine additional nights followed, together with plays and the prose critical treatise Conjectures on Original Composition (1759). In his last years he was tied to the Welwyn living through family connections. He died at Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1765.
literary_profile: A poet of melancholy, death, and immortality in blank verse, and a critic of genius and originality; his grave meditation and his theory of the creative self mark him as a bridge to Romanticism.
stylistic_characteristics: Tumid, exclamatory blank verse of the night and the grave; rhetorical question, antithesis, and point; an introspective, brooding persona; and a taste for the sublime and the morbid.
intellectual_concerns: Death, grief, and the proof of immortality; the vanity of worldly ambition; the nature of poetic genius and originality; the self in solitude; and religious consolation against despair.
historical_significance: Night Thoughts dominated the graveyard and melancholy vogue of later eighteenth-century poetry, and his Conjectures shaped the Romantic cult of original genius and influenced writers abroad.
major_influences: Augustan debates on wit and learning
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, commonly given as 1683 but sometimes earlier; the precise chronology of his Oxford preferment and family tragedies rests partly on his own partly fictionalised accounts.

literary_identity: English poet and scholar, Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is among the most quoted poems in the language.
biography: Gray was born in London and educated at Eton and at Peterhouse, Cambridge, where he later returned as a scholar and, from 1768, held the Professorship of Modern History. A careful, slow writer of small output, he published little in his lifetime, including the Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College and the Hymn to Adversity. His finest Pindaric odes, The Progress of Poesy and The Bard, appeared in 1757. His Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) brought him fame. He declined the laureateship and lived a studious, largely private life, close to a circle that included Horace Walpole. He died at Cambridge in 1771.
literary_profile: A poet of the graveyard, the meditative ode, and antiquarian romance; he combined neoclassical polish with a new interest in melancholy, the common dead, and the music and history of earlier English and Welsh verse.
stylistic_characteristics: Exquisite diction and sonorous, Latinate word order; a restrained, melancholy dignity; Pindaric and Norse-influenced ode experiments; and an antiquarian taste for the ballad and the picturesque.
intellectual_concerns: Unfulfilled potential and the fate of obscure lives; death, memory, and the moral lesson of the grave; the history and progress of poetry; and the aesthetics of melancholy and the sublime.
historical_significance: The Elegy became the landmark of the graveyard school and a touchstone of sensibility, while his odes and editorial interests in old poetry helped open the way to Romantic and antiquarian taste.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1716, but some records support 1717; the dating of the Elegy's composition, long associated with the churchyard at Stoke Poges, is debated.

literary_identity: English lyric poet of the Odes, associated with Gray and with the rise of imaginative, impassioned, and personified poetry.
biography: Collins was born at Chichester, the son of an insurer, and studied at Winchester College and at Queen's College, Oxford. A volume of odes appeared in 1746 but sold poorly and was effectively withdrawn, and the pieces came to be prized chiefly after his death. Later poems such as Ode on the Poetical Character and his oriental and Persian imitations mark his range. Mental illness and early death cut short his career; he was tended in his last years by his lifelong friend the painter Joseph Hammell, and he died at Chichester in 1759. Gray, who admired him, did much to secure his posthumous reputation.
literary_profile: A short-lived lyric poet whose best work casts abstract qualities as personified figures in an atmosphere of imaginative reverie, enthusiasm, and melancholy; he stands between the Augustans and the pre-Romantics.
stylistic_characteristics: Rich, sustained personification; lyric and ode measures of great musicality; elevated, sometimes archaic diction; and an intoxicating, enthusiastic imaginative tone distinct from Pope's point.
intellectual_concerns: The power of imagination and poetic enthusiasm; the personified emotions and qualities of the mind; the appeal of the exotic, the supernatural, and melancholy; and the poet's isolation.
historical_significance: One of the most important lyric poets between Pope and the Romantics; his odes were championed by Samuel Johnson and later admired for prefiguring Romantic imagination and sensibility.
biographical_uncertainty: The number and publication history of his odes are complicated by the suppression of his 1746 volume and later editorial reconstruction; the nature and onset of his mental illness are imperfectly documented.

literary_identity: English poet and physician, author of the philosophical poem The Pleasures of Imagination, an early statement of associationist aesthetics.
biography: Akenside was born at Newcastle, the son of a butcher of Dissenting inclinations, and was educated at a Dissenting academy and then at the University of Edinburgh and Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and turned to medicine. He practised in various English towns and at length in London. His three-book philosophical poem The Pleasures of Imagination appeared in 1744 and was revised in 1763, making his reputation. He also wrote odes and medical and political verse. A Fellow of the Royal Society, he took a medical degree at Leiden late in life. He died in 1770.
literary_profile: A didactic poet of taste and the mind who treats the imagination philosophically, drawing on associationist psychology, Shaftesburian moral sense, and the language of the sublime and the beautiful.
stylistic_characteristics: Miltonic blank verse of stately length; philosophical paraphrase and abstraction; personification of mental powers; and an elevated, rhapsodic, sometimes diffuse didactic manner.
intellectual_concerns: The nature and training of taste; the association of ideas; beauty, sublimity, and the pleasures of the mind; moral sense and virtue; and the relation of imagination to truth and feeling.
historical_significance: The Pleasures of Imagination is a key early work of eighteenth-century aesthetic theory in verse, transmitting Shaftesbury, Addison, and associationism to a poetic audience and influencing later aesthetic thought.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1721 but sometimes 1722; the details of his medical practice and his London hospital connections are only partly documented.

literary_identity: English poet and gardener, of the Leasowes, a pastoral writer and letter-writer whose ornamental garden became an eighteenth-century landmark of taste.
biography: Shenstone was born into the Worcestershire gentry, educated at Halesowen and at Pembroke College, Cambridge, and succeeded to the family estate, the Leasowes, which he laid out as a celebrated ornamental farm. He wrote the pastoral poem The Schoolmistress (1742) and other pastorals, songs, and epistles, publishing his Poetical Works in a collected form in 1763. His letters and his critical and horticultural writings circulated among friends and were partly printed after his death, notably his account of the Leasowes and his essays on taste and gardening. He died unmarried at the Leasowes in 1763.
literary_profile: A poet of retirement, rural sympathy, and sensibility, and a practised maker of landscapes; his verse and his garden together embody the cult of the picturesque and the ornamented farm.
stylistic_characteristics: Gentle, conversational pastoral and occasional verse; Spenserian and Thomsonian descriptive influence; a warm, familiar, sometimes digressive epistolary prose; and an aesthetic of artless variety.
intellectual_concerns: Rural life and the education of rustic minds; taste, the picturesque, and the design of landscapes; retirement, friendship, and benevolence; and the integration of art and nature.
historical_significance: A central figure in the development of the English landscape garden and picturesque taste, and a respected pastoral and epistolary writer linking Thomson's nature poetry to later sensibility.
biographical_uncertainty: His exact birthplace is given variously in accounts of the Worcestershire parish; the precise dating of his garden improvements and of the circulation of his letters and essays remains partly conjectural.

literary_identity: English poet, dramatist, and garden theorist, author of blank-verse tragedy and essays on poetry and gardening, associated with pre-Romantic sensibility.
biography: Mason, sometimes called the younger to distinguish him from a kinsman of the same name, was educated at Westminster School and Queen's College, Oxford, and inherited an estate at Nuthall in Nottinghamshire. His Poems (1754) won immediate attention, and he followed with elegiac and didactic verse, including essays on eclogues and on garden design. He turned to blank-verse historical tragedy with Elfrida (1763) and Caractacus (1769), and he wrote a Life of his friend Thomas Gray. A keen gardener and man of letters, he corresponded widely within the literary circles of the age. He died at Nuthall in 1797.
literary_profile: A poet, dramatist, and man of letters whose work spans the sentimental elegy, the garden essay, and declamatory blank-verse tragedy, reflecting the movement from Augustan taste toward pre-Romantic feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Correct, elevated blank verse; didactic ease in the essay poem; mournful sensibility in the elegy; and a rhetorical, declamatory grandeur in the tragedies, with a cultivated taste for the picturesque garden.
intellectual_concerns: Taste and the design of gardens; moral and heroic virtue in historical drama; friendship, biography, and literary memory; melancholy, retirement, and religious consolation.
historical_significance: A transitional figure of later-eighteenth-century letters whose garden writings and blank-verse tragedy reflect the spread of picturesque taste and pre-Romantic sensibility; his Life of Gray is an important literary document.
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace is given variously in biographical accounts; the precise chronology of his poems and essays, and his relation to the older William Mason of the same family, require careful distinction.

literary_identity: Scottish Church of Scotland minister and poet, author of the meditative grave-poem The Grave, a landmark of the graveyard school.
biography: Blair was born about 1699 and was ordained a minister of the Church of Scotland, where he became associated with the more liberal, Moderate interest in the kirk. He is remembered above all for his blank-verse poem The Grave (1743), a somber meditation on death and the resurrection that went through many editions and influenced the grave poetry that followed. He published sermons and devotional writings, but The Grave was his only poem of lasting note. He died in 1746.
literary_profile: A minister-poet whose single enduring work, The Grave, gives the eighteenth-century meditation on mortality an elevated, didactic, and pictorial blank-verse form.
stylistic_characteristics: Grave, sonorous blank verse; accumulated images of burial, decay, and resurrection; sermon-like urgency; and a sustained mood of solemn meditation rather than narrative or wit.
intellectual_concerns: Death, the grave, and the hope of resurrection; the vanity of worldly distinctions before death; the equality of all in the tomb; and Christian consolation and judgement.
historical_significance: The Grave is a defining text of the graveyard school, alongside Young's Night Thoughts, shaping the later-eighteenth-century poetics of melancholy and mortality; Blair also belongs to the Moderate current of the Scottish kirk.
major_influences: the sermon and sacred meditation tradition
biographical_uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain and variously recorded; details of his Scottish charges and of the early illustration history of The Grave are imperfectly established.

literary_identity: Welsh-born poet and painter, associated with Thomson and the descriptive school, author of Grongar Hill and the georgic The Fleece.
biography: Dyer was a Welshman, born about 1700, who first trained for a profession connected with architecture and surveying before turning to painting and poetry in the artistic circle around James Thomson and the Burlington set. His topographical poem Grongar Hill (1726) celebrates a Welsh landscape in light-reflective blank verse. He travelled in Italy and, back in Wales, farmed and wrote, producing the georgic The Fleece (1757), a poem on the Welsh wool trade. Weak memory and modest means marked his later years. He died in 1758.
literary_profile: A poet of landscape and the visual, whose descriptive and georgic verse reflects a painter's eye for colour, distance, and light and a patriot's attachment to Welsh scenery and industry.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, pictorial blank verse of space and colour; a sense of the distance and depth of a prospect; ease in the topographical and georgic mode; and a calm, contemplative, sensuous eye.
intellectual_concerns: The perception of landscape, distance, and light; patriotic and economic interest in the Welsh wool trade; retirement and rural labour; and the interplay of painting and poetry.
historical_significance: Grongar Hill is an early, much-admired poem of the picturesque prospect and a precursor of Romantic nature perception; Dyer helped link Thomson's descriptive verse to a Welsh topographical tradition.
biographical_uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain, given only as about 1700; the details of his early training and his later farming and mental decline rest on fragmentary accounts.

literary_identity: English poet and forger, the marvellous boy, whose fabricated medieval Rowley poems and tragic early death made him a Romantic legend.
biography: Chatterton was born in Bristol into a poor musical family and, as a boy connected with the church of St Mary Redcliffe, he discovered old manuscript documents he claimed were the work of a fifteenth-century monk, Thomas Rowley. From these he forged an entire pseudo-antique body of verse in a convincing archaic diction. He moved to London in 1770 to seek patronage and made a precarious living as a reporter and hack, also writing learned essays and poetry. Neglected and despairing, he died in London in 1770 by arsenic poisoning, aged seventeen. His story and the Rowley poems were taken up by Horace Walpole and later by the Romantics.
literary_profile: A poet of astonishing early gift who invented a medieval voice and persona; the Rowley pieces mix archaic pastiche with genuine lyric feeling, and his own later verse anticipates the grave and melancholy modes.
stylistic_characteristics: Ingenious Rowley archaism of invented Middle-English diction; ballad and hymn measures; and in his modern verse a meditative, often melancholy descriptive and personifying style.
intellectual_concerns: The authenticity and romance of the literary past; imitation and forgery; the neglected genius and the cruelty of patronage; mortality and despair; and national poetic origins.
historical_significance: The Rowley forgeries stimulated the antiquarian revival of old English poetry and helped shape the Romantic cult of the doomed child-genius; his legend, told by Wordsworth, Keats, and others, became a literary myth.
biographical_uncertainty: The circumstances and even the date of his death by suicide are partly legendary; the exact nature of the parish documents behind the Rowley forgeries is known chiefly from Chatterton's own unreliable accounts.

literary_identity: Scottish scholar and literary forger, the Ossian, whose claimed ancient Gaelic epics won European fame and a long authenticity controversy.
biography: Macpherson was born in Inverness-shire, educated briefly at Aberdeen and Edinburgh, and worked as a schoolmaster while collecting Highland ballads and Gaelic fragments. With the encouragement of Hugh Blair and other patrons he published Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760), followed by Fingal (1761) and the epic Temora (1763), presented as translations of the ancient bard Ossian. The works were translated across Europe and admired by many, while critics, notably Samuel Johnson, charged him with forgery. He used the fame and a government pension to secure posts in colonial administration and later sat in the British Parliament. He died in 1796.
literary_profile: A maker of pseudo-primitive epic; his translations of Ossian offer a vast, dim, elegiac world of heroes, ghosts, and landscapes in a singularly hypnotic, rhythmic prose-poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: High, cadenced, repetitive prose-verse; invocations, apostrophe, and broken parallelism; an intentionally archaic, primitive sublimity and melancholy.
intellectual_concerns: National and Celtic origins of poetry; primitive genius and the sublime of the elder world; memory, loss, and the passing of heroes; and the authenticity of literary tradition.
historical_significance: The Ossianic vogue was a European literary event that fed Romantic primitivism, melancholy, and nationalist epic; the ensuing forgery debate sharpened ideas of authenticity and folk-poetry collection.
biographical_uncertainty: His exact date and place of birth are given as 1736 in Inverness-shire but only approximately; the degree to which he worked from genuine Gaelic tradition versus pure invention remains contested.

literary_identity: English scholar, bishop, and antiquary whose Reliques of Ancient English Poetry revived the ballad and shaped the study of old English verse.
biography: Percy, born in Shropshire to a modest family, was educated at school in Shrewsbury and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. In 1765 he published the Reliques of Ancient English Poetry, drawing on an old manuscript folio of ballads, which set off a great vogue for the popular ballad and influenced poets from Cowper and Burns to the Romantics. He edited and translated northern and antique material, including Five Pieces of Runic Poetry (1763) and a translation of Paul-Henri Mallet's Northern Antiquities, and prefaced the Reliques with a learned essay on the ancient minstrels. Advanced in the Irish church, he became Bishop of Dromore, where he died in 1789.
literary_profile: An antiquary-bishop and editor whose taste for the ballad, romance, and the early popular poetry of Britain made him a pivotal figure in the recovery and celebration of native literary tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: In the Reliques, a taste for the simple lyric and the harmony of old ballads; in his own verse, easy, sometimes humorous antique and pastoral imitation; and a scholarly, glossarial editorial method.
intellectual_concerns: The native and popular origins of English poetry; ballad and romance as genres; national and northern literary antiquities; and the history and manners of the minstrels and their patrons.
historical_significance: The Reliques is one of the most influential anthologies in English literary history, launching the ballad revival, aiding the Romantic revaluation of popular poetry, and stimulating Burns and the later folk movement.
biographical_uncertainty: His exact birthplace in Shropshire is given variously; the extent to which he silently revised and modernised the old ballads in the Reliques, rather than reproducing them, has long been debated.

literary_identity: Irish-born poet, essayist, novelist, and dramatist, a central figure of the London literary world, author of The Deserted Village, The Vicar of Wakefield, and She Stoops to Conquer.
biography: Goldsmith was born in rural Ireland, the son of a clergyman, and studied medicine, spending time at Edinburgh and at a continental university before taking his degree; much of his student career is legendary. He went to London to live by his pen, working as an apothecary's assistant, a hack-writer, and a tutor, and became part of the group that founded The Club with Samuel Johnson and others. He wrote and edited widely, including the cosmopolitan essays The Citizen of the World (1760-1761). His poem The Traveller (1764), his novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), and the longer The Deserted Village (1770) established his fame, and his comedy She Stoops to Conquer (1773) revived laughter on the stage. He also wrote histories and natural histories. He died in London in 1774.
literary_profile: A writer of pastoral poetry, sentimental fiction, and laughing comedy who idealises rural abundance, childhood, and Christian innocence, and who attacks luxury, depopulation, and fashionable sentimental comedy on the stage.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, mellifluous heroic couplets in the pastoral poems; a warm, simple, often self-mocking prose; and easy, generous, laughing dramatic dialogue.
intellectual_concerns: Rural depopulation, luxury, and empire; the virtues of childhood and Christian simplicity; the rivalry between laughing and sentimental comedy; and the cosmopolitan comparison of nations and manners.
historical_significance: One of the most widely read writers of the later eighteenth century, in poetry, novel, and comedy alike; The Deserted Village became a touchstone of anti-commercial nostalgia, and his comedy redirected the English stage.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, given as 1728 or 1730, and his exact Irish birthplace and his scattered university career are partly mythologised by later accounts, especially by his friend and biographer Johnson.

literary_identity: English poet, scholar, and editor, a brilliant and erratic man of letters whose religious hymns, especially Song to David, make him a singular visionary voice.
biography: Smart was born in Kent, educated at Cambridge, and took holy orders. A fine Hebrew and classical scholar, he lived in London as an editor, schoolmaster, and hack writer, and edited early plays and other texts. His great religious poem, Song to David (1763), was published amid a reputation for madness, and in 1763 he was confined in a private madhouse for some years, during which he wrote the wild private poem Jubilate Agno in a manuscript not printed until the twentieth century. Released in later life, he continued to write and edit and was eventually admitted to an institutional charity for the poor. He died in 1771 of exhaustion.
literary_profile: A poet of intense religious enthusiasm and metrical experiment, whose verse praises the created world and its Creator with an incantatory, cataloguing energy; he also edited, translated, and wrote in prose.
stylistic_characteristics: Irregular, energetic metrical vitality; antiphonal and parallel religious praise; catalogues of creatures and things; Hebrew and liturgical influence; and a visionary, sometimes deranged sublimity of imagery.
intellectual_concerns: Divine praise through the natural world; enthusiasm, reason, and madness; the sanctity of language and naming; liberty and the animal creation; and the poet's suffering and consolation.
historical_significance: Long undervalued, Smart is now recognised as one of the most original religious and visionary poets of the century, a forerunner of Romantic interest in the irrational and a master of ecstatic hymnody.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1722 from baptismal records; the chronology of his confinement and the survival and dating of the Jubilate Agno manuscript are complex and partly reconstructed.

literary_identity: English poet and hymn-writer of the evangelical and sentimental age, whose Task and Olney Hymns opened a new nature poetry and whose life was marked by depression and religious terror.
biography: Cowper was born in Hertfordshire, the son of a clergyman, was called to the bar, and after a breakdown and an attempt at self-destruction found a measure of religious assurance in evangelical Christianity. He lived much of his life in retirement under the shelter of the Hill family, at Olney and later in Norfolk. With John Newton he contributed to the Olney Hymns (1779), writing such hymns as God Moves in a Mysterious Way. His long conversational poem The Task (1785) established his fame, followed by translations of Homer and shorter poems including The Castaway and an account of his despair. Plagued all his life by melancholy and by a recurring conviction of reprobation, he died in 1800.
literary_profile: A poet of retirement, domestic life, nature, and religious feeling, who combined the descriptive, meditative, and comic-familiar modes and wrote with startling honesty of depression and faith.
stylistic_characteristics: Smooth, conversational blank verse of the familiar line; descriptive tenderness and homely humour; a passionate, troubled religious lyricism; and a gift for hymn and melancholy song.
intellectual_concerns: Providence, evangelical assurance, and despair; the consolation of rural and domestic life; anti-slavery and humane feeling; nature, retirement, and melancholy; and the critique of luxury and city life.
historical_significance: A leading poet of sensibility and the evangelical revival and one of the most influential nature poets before the Romantics, admired by Wordsworth and Coleridge for the honesty and feeling of his verse.
biographical_uncertainty: A lifelong fear of eternal reprobation makes his own accounts of his religious states hard to date precisely; the chronology of his breakdowns and his late poem on despair is partly conjectural.

literary_identity: Scottish poet in English and in the Scots dialect, celebrated for songs, narrative, and lyric, and honoured as the national poet of Scotland.
biography: Burns was born in Ayrshire to a poor tenant farmer and was largely educated at home and by informal tutoring, working the land from childhood. His Kilmarnock edition, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (1786), was an immediate success and took him to Edinburgh, where he moved among literary and aristocratic circles. Later he settled as an officer of excise and continued to collect and adapt Scottish songs, contributing to James Johnson's Musical Museum and to George Thomson's collections. His lyrics and songs, and his narrative and satiric poems, such as Tam o' Shanter (1790) and Holy Willie's Prayer, display a range of humour, sentiment, and radical sympathy. He died in Dumfries in 1796, aged thirty-seven.
literary_profile: A poet and songwriter of the common tongue, equally at home in tender lyric, bawdy, comic narrative, and democratic or religious satire, drawing on the native Scottish song and vernacular tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: Vivid Scots vernacular diction and idiom; song-measures of great melodic fluency; direct, passionate, and often humorous address; and a blend of rustic naturalness with refined lyric sensibility.
intellectual_concerns: Common humanity and democratic fellow-feeling; the critique of religious hypocrisy and cant; the value of nature and vernacular song; nationality, friendship, and the dignity of the ordinary.
historical_significance: The national poet of Scotland and a seminal figure of the Romantic age and of vernacular and song literature; he elevated Scottish dialect poetry and became a global emblem of popular, egalitarian feeling.
biographical_uncertainty: The authorship and dating of individual songs are often complicated by his free borrowing, adaptation, and reconstruction of traditional texts; some details of his political sympathies are disputed.

literary_identity: English poet, essayist, lexicographer, and critic, the dominant man of letters of later-eighteenth-century England.
biography: Johnson was born at Lichfield, studied at Pembroke College, Oxford, and after a brief schoolmastership returned to the Midlands before going to London to live by his pen. He wrote for the Gentleman's Magazine, and as editor produced the dictionary that defined English for a century, A Dictionary of the English Language (1755). Between 1750 and 1752 he wrote the moral weekly The Rambler, and later contributed to other periodicals including The Idler; the philosophical tale The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia appeared in 1759. His poetry includes London (1738) and The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). A devoted Tory and Anglican and a founding member of The Club, he edited Shakespeare (1765) and wrote the Journey to the Western Islands (1775) and the Lives of the English Poets (1779-1781). He died in London in 1784.
literary_profile: A moralist, critic, and lexicographer of immense range, who practised the periodical essay, didactic verse, dictionary-making, textual editing, and biography, always subordinating fancy to judgement and common sense.
stylistic_characteristics: Latinate, balanced, periodic prose of antithesis and generalisation; the weighty heroic couplet of his moral verse; a sententious, authoritative, common-sense tone; and a preference for truth over ornament.
intellectual_concerns: The regulation of the passions and the vanity of worldly hopes; the stability and authority of language; the criticism of literature by general nature; religion, duty, and mortality; and the common life.
historical_significance: The most authoritative English literary voice of his age, whose dictionary standardised the language and whose criticism set the terms for assessing poetry and the canon well into the nineteenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: A probable congenital condition and an uncertain recovery from scrofula are described in accounts that mix fact with family legend; the dating of his early marriage and his first London writings is imperfect.

literary_identity: Scottish lawyer and autobiographer, immortal as the biographer and companion of Samuel Johnson and as a diarist of his own life and times.
biography: Boswell was born in Edinburgh, the son of a judge, Lord Auchinleck, and was called to the Scottish bar. A restless, self-analysing young man, he travelled widely and met David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau before becoming, in 1763, Johnson's devoted friend and would-be biographer. He wrote essays for his own periodical The Hypochondriack and travelled to London and to Corsica, recording a Journal of a Tour to Corsica (1768) with admiration for its patriots, and later a Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785) with Johnson. His masterpiece, The Life of Samuel Johnson, appeared in 1791. In later years he lived at the family estate of Auchinleck and died in London in 1795; his frank private journal was printed only in the twentieth century.
literary_profile: A biographer, diarist, and essayist whose genius was for recording speech, personality, and the texture of daily life; his journals and Life of Johnson founded modern biographical and autobiographical realism.
stylistic_characteristics: Vivid, intimate, anecdotal prose; faithful reproduction of talk and character; a self-exposing, confessional diary manner; and a mixture of Scotticism with cultivated Augustan ease.
intellectual_concerns: The study of character and genius; friendship, emulation, and self-knowledge; nationality, law, and politics; and the value of the everyday and the documentary record.
historical_significance: His Life of Johnson and his rediscovered journals make him a founder of modern biography and autobiography and one of the most valuable witnesses to eighteenth-century literary and social life.
major_influences: David Hume and the Scottish Enlightenment

literary_identity: Scottish Presbyterian minister, rhetorician, and literary critic of the Scottish Enlightenment, the first professor of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at Edinburgh.
biography: Blair was born in Edinburgh, studied divinity there, and was ordained to a ministry in the Church of Scotland, rising to the leading Edinburgh congregations and becoming a prominent figure of the Moderate interest. He lectured on rhetoric and belles lettres and was appointed to the newly created chair of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at the University of Edinburgh in 1762. His best-known work, Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, was published in 1783, drawing on decades of teaching and becoming a standard text on taste, style, and criticism. He wrote influential sermons and critical essays, and his endorsements figured in the literary debates over Ossian and the ballad. He died in 1800.
literary_profile: A critic, rhetorician, and preacher who codified Enlightenment ideas of taste, style, and eloquence, defending polite letters, sensible religion, and the analysis of beautiful writing.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, measured, authoritative critical prose of definition, example, and classification of styles; a temperate homiletic voice in the sermons; and an emphasis on perspicuity, harmony, and decorum.
intellectual_concerns: The nature of taste, genius, and the sublime; rhetoric and the principles of eloquence; the history and criticism of style and genres; and the alliance of politeness with reasonable religion and morality.
historical_significance: A defining voice of the Moderate wing of the Scottish Enlightenment; his Lectures standardised rhetorical and literary-critical teaching for a century, and his judgments shaped taste in the Ossian and ballad debates.
major_influences: George Campbell and the new rhetoric

literary_identity: English critic, playwright, and controversialist, a passionate early theorist of the sublime and one of the most quarrelsome and perceptive literary minds of his age.
biography: Dennis was educated at a grammar school in Hertford and, by some accounts, at Cambridge, before briefly joining the army and then devoting himself to letters and the stage. He wrote tragedies, including Appius and Virginia (1709), and many critical works, among them The Advancement and Reformation of Poetry and Music (1701), The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry (1704), and treatises on the sublime, the operas, and the stage. He anticipated the Romantic enthusiasm he preached, and his quarrels, notably with Addison over Cato and with Pope and Steele, made him a notorious figure. A Whig and a devoted student of French classical criticism and of Longinus, he championed enthusiastick poetry. He died in 1734, in poverty and mental distress.
literary_profile: An aggressive, original critic and theorist of poetry and religion who, drawing on Longinus and Boileau, argued for enthusiastic imagination and the sublime against cold neoclassical regularity.
stylistic_characteristics: Vehement, hyperbolic, often ranting critical prose; a rhetoric of enthusiasm and transports; sharp personal invective; and an earnest, sometimes incoherent eagerness in praise of the sublime.
intellectual_concerns: The sublime and enthusiastic imagination against rule; the relation of poetry to religion and passion; the defence of modern learning and national drama; and the corruption of critical taste.
historical_significance: A major forerunner of eighteenth-century and Romantic theories of the sublime and enthusiastic imagination; his critical writings, despite his notoriety, influenced Addison and later aesthetic thought.
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1657 from baptismal evidence, his exact birthplace is uncertain, and his claim to a university education rests on later testimony rather than firm records.

literary_identity: English literary historian, poet, and scholar, professor at Oxford and Poet Laureate, best known for the foundational History of English Poetry.
biography: Thomas Warton the younger, son of the poet Thomas Warton the elder and brother of the critic Joseph Warton, was educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of Oriel College and later Professor of Poetry. He published early verse, including The Pleasures of Melancholy (1747), contributed odes written jointly with his brother, and wrote an Essay on the Genius and Writings of Pope. His lifelong work, The History of English Poetry, whose first volumes appeared in 1774, 1778, and 1781, pioneered the historical study of medieval and Renaissance verse and its French and Italian sources. He became Poet Laureate in 1785. He died in 1790.
literary_profile: A poet and a literary historian of romantic and antiquarian sympathies who, reacting against strict neoclassicism, prized imagination, the medieval tale, and the historical development of national literature.
stylistic_characteristics: In his verse, a melancholy, descriptive, and occasionally antiquarian manner; in his History, a learned, digressive, source-hunting scholarly prose that valued imaginative romance and native tradition.
intellectual_concerns: The origins and historical development of English poetry; the romance tradition and its sources; the imagination versus rules; national literary identity; and the pleasures of melancholy and retirement.
historical_significance: The History of English Poetry is a founding work of English literary history and scholarship, establishing the study of medieval and early modern literature and anticipating Romantic interest in romance and imagination.
biographical_uncertainty: He must be carefully distinguished from his father and his brother Joseph, also literary figures, and his exact birthplace is given variously; the completion and dating of the later volumes of his History are uneven.

literary_identity: English poet, essayist, children's writer, and editor, a leading literary and political voice between the Augustan and the Romantic ages.
biography: Barbauld was born into a literary Dissenting family, the daughter of the teacher and historian John Aikin, and was partly educated through her family and the circle of the Warrington Academy. She married the Unitarian minister John Barbauld in 1773 and was involved in running a school kept by him. Her Poems (1773) established her reputation as a polished neoclassical writer. She became a celebrated author of children's literature with Hymns in Prose for Children and the influential Early Lessons (1778-1779), and she wrote political prose, including the pamphlet Sins of Government, Sins of the Nation (1793). She edited the anthology The British Novelists (1810) with an important prefatory essay. A long poem, Eighteen Hundred and Eleven (1812), drew hostile reviews, and she died at Stoke Newington in 1825.
literary_profile: A versatile writer of polished Augustan poetry, moral and political prose, and pioneering children's literature, whose work links the neoclassical and the Romantic, the rational and the sentimental.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, correct, often elevated couplet in her verse, marked by Pope-like balance and moral seriousness; a lucid, persuasive, and at times passionate prose; and an intimate, instructive address adapted to children.
intellectual_concerns: Liberty, dissent, and the ethics of government and war; the education and moral formation of the young; the proper objects of poetry and taste; and the relation of feeling, reason, and public duty.
historical_significance: A major woman of letters who shaped late-Augustan poetry, helped found children's educational literature in English, and influenced contemporaries; her critical and editorial work made her a central figure of her age.
major_influences: the Augustan couplet and moral essay
biographical_uncertainty: Her exact birthplace is given variously; details of her schoolwork with her husband's academy and the full extent of her editorial series are known only partly and require careful reconstruction.
